newsitem.title: USA: Clinton makes balanced budget top 2nd term item.
newsitem.headline: Clinton makes balanced budget top 2nd term item.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday told his incoming and outgoing Cabinet members that reaching agreement with the Republican-led Congress on a balanced federal budget would be a top priority of his second term.

During a seven-hour working session with them, Clinton also expressed his eagerness for an active foreign policy and to work with Congress to obtain an increase in the U.S. budget for foreign affairs.
Leaving the meeting at Blair House on a frigid day to walk back to the White House across the street Clinton, accompanied by his wife, would say only that the talks went "great."
"We'll be ready to go on the 21st," he said, referring to Jan. 21, the day after he is inaugurated for his second term.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Hillary Rodham Clinton's attendance did not signal a formal role in the administration and that she spent the entire time listening.
"She did not directly participate but was very interested in the deliberations," McCurry said.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Clinton recommitted himself to the goal of bringing the federal budget into balance by the year 2002. Attempts to reach a deal with Congress last year foundered.
Rubin quoted Clinton as saying that completing the job of balancing the budget was "critical to the administration's credibility" on all other issues.
"So clearly he made balancing the budget central to his strategy for a second term," Rubin said.
Clinton is to offer his proposed budget for the 1998 fiscal year in early February.

National Security Adviser-designate Samuel Berger said Clinton heard an impassioned plea from his secretary of state nominee, Madeleine Albright, to increase the amount of money the United States spends on foreign policy. She said words to the effect that "about 1 percent of the budget will determine 50 percent of our legacy," Berger said.
Republicans have been intent on reducing U.S. foreign aid, believing it is a waste of money. America is more than $1 billion in arrears in its dues to the United Nations.

Berger said Clinton "forsees an active foreign policy agenda" and stressed the need for a "close partnership" with Congress on foreign affairs. He said the administration would discuss with Congress ways the United Nations can reform itself in return for Washington paying its debt.

Teamwork was a frequent topic of conversation during the Cabinet retreat, which brought together outgoing Cabinet officers as well as those nominated for positions and facing Senate confirmation hearings. Vice President Al Gore and senior White House staff also attended.
Environmental Protection Administration chief Carol Browner said Clinton wanted to build on his first-term progress on environmental preservation and protection of the public health.
